description: We are a team of four Sophomores from Needham, Massachusetts. Our team specializes in skills pertaining to aerospace, data analysis, and robotics. We have multiple prior engineering competition experiences, such as receiving first place in an MIT affiliated national CubeSat challenge.
summary:
The Mars Analog Finder is a website that analyzes locations Earth and compares them to a chosen location on Mars using geological (basaltic, phyllosilicates/clay,  sulfates, carbonates, silica/evaporites), landforms & terrain (topography, aeolian bed forms, caves), climate & radiation (temperature, aridity, water availability), and water (ice, permafrost, salt deliquescnce potential, periglacial ground and gullies) criterion to identify the top 5 locations on Earth that closely resemble areas on Mars on a scale of 0 to 1. 
The identification of potential analog locations of Mars here on Earth is crucial because it allows scientists and engineers to study and test equipment in environments on Earth that closely replicate conditions on Mars before sending missions into space. For example, researchers could use locations in deserts or volcanic regions to test robotic equipment, spacesuits, and other technology that may be used during future Mars missions. Overall, the Mars Analog Finder could help ameliorate the safety of future space explorations, make the Mars planning stages more efficient, and allow scientists to understand the challenges of the Martian environment before astronauts ever arrive.
details:
Our project identifies Earth locations that are analogs of locations on Mars. It is based on a criterion system, where the criteria are different aspects that can be similar between the two planets. Our criteria are geology (basaltic, phyllosilicates/clay, sulfates, carbonates, silica/evaporites), chemical composition of the surface, temperature, ice and permafrost, dust concentrations, and caves (focused on cave entrances). They also include topography, aridity (water vapor amounts), salt deliquescence potential (how often a location is humid and cold enough that salt absorbs water), and periglacial patterned ground and gullies (whether the ground shows signs of freezing and thawing).

First, the data is taken in. For smaller datasets this is done directly; larger datasets are taken in chunks. Next, the data is parsed, which extracts the key information from each dataset at a specific location and feeds it directly into the next step, the per-criteria similarity. Each criteria has two datasets, one for Earth and one for Mars. Each criteria also has a "type," which dictates how it should work. The criteria are then given weights made up of user-inputted weights and derived weights (from standard deviation). These weights are combined with the per-criterion similarity scores through a weighted average, which yields a final similarity score from 0 to 1.

Finally, the program searches for the best location. It takes in the inputted Mars location and calls the previous steps to check the score of each Earth location. It takes a random sample of 200 Earth locations to find the standard deviation, and therefore the weights. We then keep taking measurements on finer areas of Earth, from 80 degrees down to 2.5 degrees, for efficiency. For each block and each criteria, it finds the top similarity score, which lets us look at the block with the best score at a finer degree.

The project finds the Earth locations that are the closest analogs to any chosen location on Mars and ranks them with a similarity score from 0 to 1. The results are shown in bar charts and 3D visualizations of Earth and Mars, so analog sites can be easily compared and explored.

We used 35 datasets for Earth and Mars. The similarity and weighting model is written in Python, and the website in JavaScript, HTML and CSS. CesiumJS and Cesium ion power the 3D Mars and Earth globes, Chart.js draws the bar charts, and the site is hosted on GitHub Pages.

Our project is creative because each criterion has its own "type," which dictates how the Earth and Mars data are compared. The weights combine user-inputted importance with weights derived from standard deviation, so the results change based on what the user cares about. The search also narrows from 80 degrees to 2.5 degrees for efficiency.

We decided to focus exclusively on Mars. This allows atmospheric analysis and lets us analyze ice. It also lets us gather more criteria and data for one planet rather than less data for both, and combine 35 datasets. The challenges and limitations our team faced during this challenge started with finding accurate data: locating reliable and updated geological and terrain data for both Earth and Mars. Data compatibility was also a challenge, since we had to find 35 datasets that work for both planets, and some of our criterion datasets cover only part of Mars or Earth (for example, geology carbonates on Mars). We also had to choose our criteria by deciding which factors were most important when judging whether two locations were similar. App development meant organizing large amounts of information into bar charts and 3D visualizations and making the app intuitive to navigate. It also meant downloading large datasets and connecting our data and results with our front-end UI template. Because Earth and Mars data do not always match, we sometimes had to compare relative sizes (such as cave tube diameter) instead of comparing directly. Finally, because of the time constraint, we did not have enough time to further research the Moon or add more criteria.
